title: Clap the syllables
instructions: Say each word aloud and clap its beats. Sort it by how many syllables it has.

title: Find the season
instructions: Many haiku hide a season word. Tap the two words that tell you when this haiku happens.
text:
Cold snowflakes falling
on the empty playground swings.
Winter holds its breath.
explanation: Snowflakes and winter tell us the season without a long description. Haiku poets use one season word to set the whole scene.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in each line of a haiku?
questions.explanation: A haiku has three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables: short, longer, short.

questions.prompt: What does a haiku usually capture?

options.text: A whole story with a beginning, middle and end
One small moment, often from nature, seen clearly
A list of rhyming words

questions.explanation: A haiku is like a photograph: one moment, seen so clearly the reader can step into it.

options.text: Yes, every line must rhyme
Only the first and last lines
No. Haiku count syllables, not rhymes

questions.explanation: Haiku are built on syllables and images, not rhyme. Rhyme can even make a haiku feel forced.

title: A day in three haiku
prompt: Write three haiku about one day: morning, afternoon and night. Each haiku catches one small moment you could see, hear or feel. Leave a blank line between them.
tips: 5 syllables, then 7, then 5. Watch the counter go green.
Show one moment, like a photograph. Skip the feelings words: let the picture do it.
Try a small surprise in the last line.

title: Stop or run on?
instructions: Does each line stop, or run on into the next line?

title: A word alone
instructions: The poet gave two words a line of their own. Tap them.
text:
The house was empty
and
I walked from room to room
listening
for footsteps that would never come.
explanation: A word on its own line makes the reader pause on it. “and” makes us wait; “listening” stretches the silence. Line breaks are choices.

options.text: A poem with no rhyme scheme or fixed rhythm, shaped by its line breaks
A poem that is free to read online
A poem with exactly 14 lines

questions.explanation: Free verse doesn't follow rules for rhyme or rhythm. The poet chooses where every line breaks.

questions.prompt: “I opened the box and found / nothing.” Why put “nothing” on its own line?

options.text: Because the first line was too long
To make the reader pause, then feel the surprise
Poems must have short lines

questions.explanation: The line break makes the reader wait for what's in the box, so “nothing” lands like a surprise.

questions.prompt: What does a line that runs on (no punctuation at the end) do?

options.text: Makes the reader stop for a long time
Pulls the reader into the next line, building speed or suspense
Is a mistake

questions.explanation: A run-on line (enjambment) carries the reader forward. It can build tension or make the poem flow.

title: A place I know by heart
prompt: Write a free-verse poem about a place you know by heart: your kitchen, a bus stop, a grandparent's garden, a corner of the playground. Show the place with details, and choose every line break on purpose: where should the reader pause, rush on, or stop on one word?
tips: Write it first as sentences, then break it into lines.
Try “Read with pauses” and “Read straight through” to hear your breaks.
Give your most important word a line of its own.

title: The chorus
instructions: Spoken-word poets repeat a line like a chorus. Tap the three words of the repeated phrase.
text:
I come from loud kitchens,
from Sunday songs and burnt toast.
I come from stories
told twice and laughed at three times.
I come from here.
explanation: “I come from” returns again and again, like a chorus. Repetition gives a spoken poem its heartbeat and helps listeners follow it.

title: Where's the beat?
instructions: Say each word aloud. Is the strong beat on the first syllable or the second?

questions.prompt: What makes spoken word different from a poem on the page?

options.text: It's written to be performed out loud, so rhythm and voice matter most
It never uses line breaks
It must be exactly one minute long

questions.explanation: Spoken word is poetry for the ear. Performers use rhythm, repetition, pauses and their own voice.

questions.prompt: Why do spoken-word poets repeat lines?

options.text: They forgot what they wrote
Listeners can't re-read, so repetition helps them follow and feel the beat
To make the poem longer

questions.explanation: On a page you can look back; in a performance you can't. A repeated line is an anchor for the audience.

questions.prompt: When performing, where is a good place to pause?

options.text: In the middle of a word
At a line break, or just before an important word
Never: keep going as fast as possible

questions.explanation: A pause before an important word makes the audience lean in. Line breaks show you where to breathe.

title: Where I'm from
prompt: Write a spoken-word poem called “Where I'm From”. Fill it with the sounds, foods, sayings and places that made you. Choose a line to repeat, like a chorus, and write it to be read aloud. Then try it with the beat and record yourself.
tips: Start several lines the same way: “I'm from…”.
Use details only you would know: a smell, a saying, a song.
Mark the stressed syllables and read along with the beat.

title: Name that sound
instructions: Sort each line by the sound device it uses most.

items.text: Busy bees buzz by the bench.
The kettle hisses, the toast pops.
Drip, drop, splash goes the rain.
The stars came out at night / and filled the sky with light.
I sat beside the sea / as calm as I could be.
Run, run, run, as fast as you can.
Never again, never again, I said.

title: Hear it
instructions: Tap the three words that sound like what they mean.
text: The pan began to sizzle, the door banged shut, and somewhere outside a car horn honked twice.
explanation: Sizzle, bang and honk are onomatopoeia: words that sound like the noise they describe. Read them aloud and you can hear the kitchen.

options.text: Wild wind whips the washing line.
The wind is very strong today.
The washing is drying outside.

questions.explanation: Wild, wind, whips and washing all start with the same “w” sound. That's alliteration.

questions.prompt: Why do poets use sound devices?

options.text: To make the poem longer
To make the poem fun to read aloud and to add to its mood
Because every poem must rhyme

questions.explanation: Sound devices make poems musical. Soft sounds can calm the reader; hard sounds can startle them.

questions.prompt: Which sounds best fit a calm, sleepy poem?

options.text: Crash, bang, smash
Hush, whisper, murmur
Pop, crack, snap

questions.explanation: Soft “sh” and “m” sounds feel quiet and gentle. Hard sounds like “crash” and “crack” feel loud and sudden.

title: A poem you can hear
prompt: Write a poem about a noisy (or very quiet) place: a storm, a kitchen at dinnertime, a swimming pool, a library, a city at night. Use at least three sound devices on purpose: alliteration, onomatopoeia, rhyme or repetition. Choose sounds that fit the mood.
tips: Read every line aloud as you write it.
Match the sounds to the mood: soft sounds for calm, hard sounds for chaos.
Rhyme is optional. Don't let it force a word you don't mean.
